```{r setup}
library(pilotr)
```

## The challenge

The R and Python ecosystems use different default random-number generators (R's
Mersenne-Twister with inversion, NumPy's PCG64), so a direct port produces different data from
the same seed. That would undermine the guarantee that a design authored once can be reproduced
anywhere.

## A shared generator

In place of the default generators, pilotr provides a shared generator implemented identically
in both languages. Uniform deviates come from L'Ecuyer's (1988) combined linear congruential
generator. Every intermediate product stays below $2^{53}$, so the arithmetic is exact in R's
IEEE-754 doubles and in Python integers alike. Normal deviates use Wichura's (1988) Algorithm
AS 241 inverse-CDF, the algorithm R's `qnorm()` uses. The remaining draws (Cholesky-correlated
random effects, inverse-CDF Poisson and ordinal draws, Marsaglia–Tsang gamma draws for the
Beta family, a Fisher–Yates item sampler for partial crossing) are derived from those two
through a documented, identical draw order.

As a result, given the same specification and seed, the R and Python implementations produce
identical data wherever they share a maths library, as on Linux. Continuous integration
runs every case of the parity harness there. The harness holds every case to the last bit
except the unrounded dumps of `crossed_mixed_rt`, `reading_time_continuous` and
`stress_exgaussian`, which `tools/parity/tolerance.json` allows to differ by up to 8 units in the
last place, on Linux as on any other platform.

IEEE-754 fixes the rounding of arithmetic but leaves that of `exp()`, `log()` and `pow()` to the
library. On Windows, R and Python do not share one. There, a value that passes through those
functions can differ in its last bits, and every family has such a path. The figures below were
measured on Windows 11 with R 4.6.1 and Python 3.13.

- Normal draws pass through `log()` in AS 241's tail branch, which about 15% of draws take.
  About 1.4e-5 of normal draws differed, by 1 to 3 units in the last place (ulp), so Gaussian
  data can differ too.
- Responses of the lognormal families and the ex-Gaussian differed by 1 ulp.
- An unrounded Beta response differed by up to 35 ulp.
- A discrete outcome can in principle move by a whole category, although none did in 50,000
  rows of each discrete family.

One Beta case can differ on Linux too, under R 4.6.0 or later. From that version, R's `^` computes
a cube or a fourth power by repeated multiplication, where Python calls `pow()`, as R did before.
A Beta response whose Gamma shape is exactly 1/3 or 1/4 can therefore differ in its last bits.
Such a shape needs a cell whose rows share one linear predictor, as in a Beta design with no
random effects and a linear predictor of 0, where a `phi` of 0.5 gives shapes of 1/4.

A square is computed by multiplication in both languages. R's `^` computes it that way in every
version, and Python computes a boost whose exponent is exactly 2 as `u * u`. A design with a
`phi` of 1, which gives shapes of 1/2, therefore draws the same data in both. Up to version 0.3.0,
the Python package computed that square with `pow()`, and such a design could differ in its last
bits.

Rounding has removed every continuous difference observed so far, but it guarantees nothing. A
last-bit difference can straddle a rounding boundary, and `round` is not allowed for the discrete
families. `build_spec()`, which builds the no-code app's specifications, rounds the Gaussian,
lognormal, shifted lognormal and ex-Gaussian responses to four decimals and leaves a Beta
response unrounded, for the reason `?build_spec` gives. The only way to obtain agreement to the
last bit in every family is to run both languages on a platform where they share a maths
library, outside the Beta case under R 4.6.0 or later. The section
[Scope of the guarantee](https://github.com/pablobernabeu/pilotr/blob/main/spec/SPEC.md#scope-of-the-guarantee)
of the specification gives the measurements in full.

## Determinism in R

On one platform, the same specification and seed always give the same data.

```{r}
spec <- build_spec(list(
  name = "demo", seed = 2024, design_kind = "between", n_subject = 200,
  factor_name = "group", lev1 = "a", lev2 = "b",
  intercept = 100, effect = 5, family = "gaussian",
  resp_name = "score", sigma = 10))

identical(simulate_design(spec), simulate_design(spec))
```

Across operating systems, the same holds on the terms set out above, since R takes `exp()`,
`log()` and `pow()` from the platform's maths library, as Python does.

Changing the seed changes the draws, while the structure and the ground-truth parameters stay
fixed.

```{r}
spec2 <- spec; spec2$seed <- spec$seed + 1L
identical(simulate_design(spec)$score, simulate_design(spec2)$score)
```

## The same design in Python

The Python package reads the same specification. The code below, which is not evaluated here,
shows the Python you would run. Its output matches the R data to the last bit wherever the two
share a maths library.

```python
from pilotr import simulate, load_spec

# the same design.json the R package (and the app) use
data = simulate("design.json")
```

The repository includes a parity check that compares the CSV files the R and Python demo
scripts write for six of the worked example designs, all but the ordinal and Poisson ones. It
reports the maximum absolute difference per design, reads values at the precision a written file
carries and has a tolerance of 1e-6. The table below summarises it.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
# Output of python/examples/parity_check.py --csv, precomputed and shipped with
# the package: the comparison needs both a Python and an R installation, so it
# cannot run at vignette build time.
# max_abs_diff is read as text: as a number, kable would round 4.885e-15 to 0
# and the table would claim a stricter result than the check actually produced.
knitr::kable(read.csv("parity-summary.csv",
                      colClasses = c(max_abs_diff = "character")),
             format = "html", table.attr = 'class="table data-output"')
```

The difference is exactly zero for five of the six designs. The sixth, `continuous`
(`reading_time_continuous`), has a rounded response that agrees exactly. Its continuous predictors
are unrounded, and R's CSV writer prints them to 15 significant digits. Those predictors differ by
about 5e-15. At that precision, the residual cannot be told apart from the writer's own rounding,
and the tolerance of 1e-6 is there to absorb it. The parity check can be rerun on any new
platform, so a design verified on a laptop can be confirmed on an HPC node before a large run.

The bit-identical claim rests on a stricter check, the harness under `tools/parity/`. It dumps
every value at 17 significant digits, which shows whether the values themselves differ. It
accounts for each differing cell in units in the last place against a recorded allowance and must
pass in continuous integration. On Windows, it finds a handful of cells one unit in the last place
apart, from `exp()`, and no categorical mismatches. On Linux, where it runs in continuous
integration, every cell agrees. The uniform stream is exact by construction. The harness checks
the Gaussian cases against recorded hashes in `tools/parity/golden.json`, relying on the observed
agreement of AS 241's `log()` across platforms. The cases are small enough that none has met one
of the rare normal draws that differ. The cases whose values pass through `exp()`, `log()` or
`pow()` on the way to the response have no recorded hashes, because the maths library determines
those last bits. They must still pass the cross-language comparison on every run.

## The analysis layer

`solve_curve()` fits a model to a curve that has already been simulated, and it is held to a
different standard from the generator. Its fit calls `exp()` and the normal distribution function
at every iteration. A recorded hash would therefore be valid only for the maths library that
produced it, and the two engines cannot be expected to agree to the last bit. They must instead
agree far more closely than any reading of the result could depend on. The script
`tools/parity/solve_cross.py` puts the same fixed curves through both engines and compares the
solved value, its interval, the fitted coefficients and the text of a selection of error
messages. Each of those error messages is identical character for character. The largest
relative difference measured over those curves is about 5e-15, against an allowance of 1e-9. On a
solved sample size of 220 subjects, that allowance comes to two ten-millionths of a subject.

The mixed models of the two `power_mixed()` functions come from `model_formula()` and
`model_data()`, which the Python package ports from this one. The script
`tools/parity/formula_cross.py` gives the Python ports the data R simulated for every worked
example and parity case. Both packages must write the same formula character for character and the
same contrast and product columns bit for bit. The fits that follow can differ. `lme4` and
`statsmodels` are different programs, this package estimates the random-effect correlations that
the Python one leaves out, and the two test with different statistics. The Python power guide sets
out where their results diverge.

`power_report()` writes a sample-size justification from a result's counts of significant
replicates and of the replicates behind each rate. It computes each Monte Carlo error with the
functions both packages use to compute these errors, which return the same doubles for the same
counts, and formats the errors in the same way. The script `tools/parity/report_cross.py` renders
a set of stored records in both engines and requires the same text, byte for byte.

## Why this matters

Because every implementation must follow the specification and the generator is shared, a
design authored once in the app, in R or in Python can be reproduced everywhere. It can be
preregistered as a small JSON file that anyone can run, scaled from a laptop to a cluster and
handed between collaborators who work in different languages. Its data agree to the last bit
wherever the machines share a maths library.
